summary: Kole Jain argues that strong UI/UX designers focus on making things work for the user rather than on making them look good, and treat web design as a story that guides someone to an action. Using an Airbnb-like vacation rental flow, he shows how to start from user intent (a search bar first, then listings and filters for people who want to browse) and to expand functionality only as intent expands. He recommends following the layouts users already expect, choosing and structuring content for how people scan it and for imperfect real content, and using animation only when it adds clarity or function, with progressive disclosure and a Load more button over infinite scroll as examples. He closes by saying a design system should reflect the team's values and size, that developing it (rules, spacing, type scales, interaction patterns) is often more critical than the design itself, that it is a shared language rather than a way to make everything look the same, and that its rules should be broken only on purpose. For someone building a design system, this gives a user-intent-first process, content stress tests, a functional-motion stance and a way to size the system to the team.
key_ideas: Good design focuses on making things work brilliantly for the user, not only on making them look good.
Think of web design as a story that guides someone to an action; extra flare like 3D graphics or smooth scrolling can get in the way.
Start from user intent: if people come to search, the search bar is the natural starting point, augmented with useful inputs.
A site can serve more than one intent, such as searching and browsing, and each intent adds its own functionality.
Fonts, colors and icons change the aesthetics but do very little to change functionality.
Users expect certain layouts after decades of websites: top-to-bottom, left-to-right flow, navigation at the top, easy-to-find calls to action.
Conventional layouts are easier to extend with new sections and to make responsive; uniqueness comes from micro interactions and features.
Designing around content has two steps: decide what content to show, then structure it so imperfect content still works.
Animations should add clarity or functionality; his old portfolio, whose animations didn't do anything, is his example of what not to do.
Progressive disclosure shows what the user needs and reveals more as it is required.
A Load more button is preferable to infinite scroll because it gives control and lets users reach the footer.
Buttons should almost always have a small animation, while scrolljacking should be used very sparingly, if ever.
A design system should match the team: lightweight and easy to scrap for a lean startup, massive and deeply defined for many products.
Building the system (rules, spacing, typography scales, interaction patterns) is often more critical than the design itself.
A design system is a shared language, not a way to make everything look the same; break its rules with intention.

topics.name: Design process

topics.name: Design taste and judgement

rules.rule: Start a flow from the user's intent and build the element that serves it first (for a rental search, the search bar with destination, number of travelers and dates) before working on icons or card layouts.
rules.why: Starting with icons or card layouts loses the plot of why you are designing; the intent to search makes the search bar the natural starting point.
rules.evidence: Start with user intent

rules.rule: Do not add a header and background image (or similar decoration) around a core element unless it does something for the user.
rules.why: The decorated version does nothing extra that the plain version didn't.
rules.evidence: put a header above this and slap an image on the background

rules.rule: Skip flare such as 3D graphics or buttery smooth scrolling when the page's goal is to guide someone to an action.
rules.why: Not every story needs it, and all that flare might just be in the way of the action.
rules.evidence: not every story needs 3D graphics or buttery smooth scrolling

rules.rule: Add functionality only when a new user intent calls for it, for example listings plus filtering UI for people who come to browse rather than search.
rules.why: Only as the user intent expands should the functionality of the design expand; styling alone changes little about function.
rules.evidence: Only as the user intent expands do we expand the functionality of our designs

rules.rule: Follow expected layout conventions: let information flow top to bottom and left to right, put navigation at the top of the page, and make calls to action eye-catching and easy to find.
rules.why: Users have come to expect these layouts, and designs that follow them are much easier to extend with new sections and make responsive.
rules.evidence: typically information should flow top to bottom and left to right

rules.rule: Make a conventional layout your own through a micro interaction or a set of unique features rather than by abandoning expected layouts.
rules.why: Respecting expectations while adding something unique is what separates the good from the genius.
rules.evidence: Respecting these expectations, but making the design uniquely yours

rules.rule: Choose what a card shows from how users will interact with it: put the specifics people scan by (location, rating, price) on listing cards and leave detailed descriptions for the page they open on click.
rules.why: Users who want a detailed look will click the listing; they need the scannable specifics before anything else.
rules.evidence: They need the specifics to scan like the location, rating, and price before anything else

rules.rule: Test layouts with imperfect content and truncate long names such as a destination with a really long title.
rules.why: Designs built on perfect, short content end up with unintended consequences when real content arrives.
rules.evidence: We'd probably want to truncate long names

rules.rule: Put a circle behind icons that sit on photos (such as a save icon on bright listing images).
rules.why: The circle guarantees contrast whatever the image behind it.
rules.evidence: add a circle to the icon to guarantee contrast

rules.rule: Only add an animation when it adds clarity or functionality; remove animations that don't do anything.
rules.why: He shows his old portfolio website, calls it awful, and says none of its animations did anything.
rules.evidence: Animations should add clarity or functionality to a design

rules.rule: When navigation links run out of room, consolidate them into a menu that animates in.
rules.why: The menu's animation then serves a purpose instead of being decoration.
rules.evidence: we consolidate them into a menu that can animate in serving a purpose

rules.rule: When a web app takes on a browsing priority, shrink the search bar instead of sticking the whole search block to the top, and animate it open when clicked.
rules.why: The source gives it as an example of progressive disclosure: showing the user what they need to see and revealing more as it's required.
rules.evidence: reduce the size of the search bar and have it animate in when clicked

rules.rule: Use progressive disclosure: show the user what they need to see and reveal more as it is required.
rules.why: Menus and search bars that animate in on demand are given as great examples of this.
rules.evidence: showing the user what they need to see and revealing more as it's required

rules.rule: Prefer a Load more button over infinite scroll for long lists.
rules.why: It gives the user more control and lets them actually reach the footer, which infinite scroll often makes impossible.
rules.evidence: a load more button is preferable over infinite scroll

rules.rule: Give buttons a small animation.
rules.why: Given as a general rule under the principle that animation should add clarity or functionality; the source adds that context matters.
rules.evidence: buttons should almost always have a small animation

rules.rule: Avoid scrolljacking effects; use them very sparingly, if ever.
rules.why: Stated as a general rule alongside the principle that animation must add clarity or function.
rules.evidence: scrolljacking effects should be used very sparingly, if ever

rules.rule: Make the design system reflect the values of the team and size it to match: a lean startup might need one that is lightweight, flexible, quick to update and easy to scrap; a system whose use cases span dozens of products and billions of users, like Material Design, is massive and deeply defined.
rules.why: The source states the system has to reflect the values of the team, and explains Material Design's size by the number of products and users it serves.
rules.evidence: But the system has to reflect the values of the team

rules.rule: Put real effort into defining the system's rules, spacing, typography scales and interaction patterns, not only into how it looks.
rules.why: The process of defining them gives you an architecture for expansion, and the development of a design system is often more critical than the design itself.
rules.evidence: The process of defining rules, spacing, typography scales, interaction patterns gives you an architecture for expansion

rules.rule: Treat the design system as the team's shared language, not as a way to make everything look the same.
rules.why: The source says that is what a design system is about, and that mastering the language includes knowing when to bend its rules.
rules.evidence: a design system isn't about making everything look the same

rules.rule: Break a design system rule only on purpose, never by accident.
rules.why: The system is a shared language, and mastery means knowing when to bend the rules with intention.
rules.evidence: You don't break the system by accident. You break it with intention.

decisions.question: How should long lists of results load?

options.name: Load more button
options.effect: The user decides when to see more and can reach the footer.
options.when: The source's general preference for lists such as listings.

options.name: Infinite scroll
options.effect: Content keeps loading as the user scrolls, which often makes the footer impossible to reach and gives the user less control.

decisions.recommendation: Load more, because it gives the user more control and lets them reach the footer.
decisions.evidence: a load more button is preferable over infinite scroll

decisions.question: Should every option and element be visible at once, or revealed as needed?

options.name: Show everything
options.effect: All navigation links and the full search block stay on screen; with many links you run out of room.
options.when: When there is room and nothing competes with the main intent [inferred].

options.name: Progressive disclosure
options.effect: Links fold into a menu that animates in, or the search bar shrinks and animates open when clicked; users see what they need and more appears on demand.
options.when: When links run out of room, or when browsing becomes the priority over search.

decisions.recommendation: Progressive disclosure: show what the user needs and reveal more as it is required.
decisions.evidence: These are all great examples of progressive disclosure

decisions.question: Should the page follow familiar layout conventions or try a new arrangement?

options.name: Familiar layout
options.effect: Information flows top to bottom and left to right, navigation sits at the top and calls to action are easy to find; new sections and responsive versions are easier to add.
options.when: Typically, since users have come to expect these layouts.

options.name: New layout (e.g. search bar placed lower, cards arranged differently)
options.effect: Can be done if it serves the user better, but breaks what users expect.
options.when: Only if it serves the user better.

decisions.recommendation: Respect the expected layout and make it uniquely yours with a micro interaction or unique features.
decisions.evidence: users have come to expect certain layouts

decisions.question: What should a listing card show?

options.name: Short description on every listing
options.effect: More text on each card that users who want detail would get by clicking anyway.
options.when: Not preferred by the source for a browse page.

options.name: Scannable specifics (location, rating, price)
options.effect: Users can compare listings at a glance and click for the detailed look.
options.when: When users scan a list and open items for detail.

decisions.recommendation: Show the scannable specifics first; the detail lives on the listing page.
decisions.evidence: They need the specifics to scan like the location, rating, and price

decisions.question: How large and defined should the design system be?

options.name: Lightweight and flexible
options.effect: Quick to update and easy to scrap.

options.name: Massive and deeply defined
options.effect: Covers many use cases in depth, like Google's Material Design.
options.when: When use cases span dozens of products and billions of users.

decisions.recommendation: Whichever reflects the values of the team; the source does not pick one for everyone.
decisions.evidence: Google's material design is massive and deeply defined

decisions.question: Where should animation be used?

options.name: Functional animation
options.effect: A menu or search bar animates in when needed, and buttons get a small animation; motion adds clarity or function.
options.when: Buttons almost always; menus and disclosure patterns when they serve a purpose.

options.name: Decorative or scroll-taking animation
options.effect: Animations that don't do anything (like the presenter's old portfolio) or scrolljacking effects.

decisions.recommendation: Animate only when it adds clarity or functionality.
decisions.evidence: All of these animations didn't do anything

decisions.question: Where should website navigation sit, and what happens when the links run out of room?

options.name: Top navigation
options.effect: Links sit at the top of the page, where users have come to expect navigation.
options.when: The default layout convention for websites.

options.name: Menu that animates in
options.effect: Links are consolidated into a menu that animates in, so the motion serves a purpose.
options.when: As more links are added and you run out of room.

decisions.recommendation: Keep navigation at the top of the page, and consolidate links into a menu that animates in once they run out of room.
decisions.evidence: Navigation is at the top of the page

process.detail: Ask why the user is there (e.g. to search for accommodation) before thinking about icons or card layouts.

process.step: Build the element that serves it
process.detail: Start with the natural element for that intent, such as a search bar, then augment it with useful inputs like destination, number of travelers and dates.
For users who want to browse, display listings and add filtering UI; expand functionality only as intent expands.
Let information flow top to bottom and left to right, keep navigation at the top and make calls to action easy to find; add uniqueness through micro interactions or features.
Use how the user will interact to pick the information shown, e.g. location, rating and price on cards, details on click.

process.step: Structure the content for imperfect cases
process.detail: Test with long names and bright images; truncate long names and add a circle behind icons to guarantee contrast.
Animate only what adds clarity or function: menus and search bars that reveal on demand (progressive disclosure), small button animations; avoid scrolljacking.

process.step: Build a design system that fits the team
process.detail: Define rules, spacing, typography scales and interaction patterns at a size that matches the team, and break the rules only with intention.
